narration: Everyone has a number. The amount you're supposed to have saved before you're allowed to stop working. You've seen it in a hundred headlines — a million and a half dollars, give or take. And almost nobody is anywhere near it.

sub: …and the number itself quietly stopped working.
narration: But the scary part of retirement in America isn't that people are behind on the number. It's that the number itself quietly stopped working.

heading: Why Most Americans Will Never Retire
narration: So let's actually do the math. Not the vibes — the real numbers, one line at a time.

caption: Three legs. One stool.
narration: Retirement was supposed to stand on three legs. A pension from your job. Social Security from the government. And your own savings on top.

title: Private workers with a pension (%)
narration: In 1980, most workers with a plan had a pension — a guaranteed check for life. Today, it's fewer than one in ten. The guaranteed check didn't shrink. It disappeared.
In its place, your employer handed you a 401k and wished you luck. A pension is a promise. A 401k is a bet — on the market, and on you.

caption: The government's floor
narration: Then Social Security — the leg everyone assumes will catch them. The average retired worker collects about nineteen hundred dollars a month.
Nineteen hundred and three dollars a month. Call it twenty-three thousand dollars a year. For a lot of people, that isn't a floor — it's the whole house.
The famous four percent rule tells you how big the pile must be. Want forty thousand dollars a year from savings? Divide by four percent. You need one million dollars.

title: Median retirement savings, by age
narration: And what do people actually have? The typical household aged 55 to 64, staring retirement in the face, has about a hundred and eighty-five thousand dollars.
Under the four percent rule, that produces about seven thousand four hundred dollars a year. Six hundred dollars a month, to carry you through thirty years of life.
The math asks a regular person for a million dollars. The typical near-retiree has a fraction of that. The stool doesn't wobble. It falls.
